visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: The unaffected share price is 40 and the offer is 52. What's the premium?
questions.explain: 52 ÷ 40 − 1 = 30%. Dividing the 12 by the offer price gives 23%, a common slip.
questions.explain_at: Offer price divided by the share price before the deal, minus one

questions.q: Precedents show a median of 10x LTM EBITDA. Your target has EBITDA of 60 and net debt of 150. Implied equity value?
questions.explain: 10 × 60 = 600 of enterprise value, minus 150 of net debt: 450 of equity value.
questions.explain_at: Step four: apply them to your target

questions.q: Spire's enterprise value is about £2.3bn at 8.6x EBITDA. Roughly what EBITDA does that imply?
questions.explain: £2.3bn ÷ 8.6 ≈ £270m: divide the value by the multiple to get back to the metric.
questions.explain_at: The buyers paid about eight point six times Spire's adjusted EBITDA

questions.q: Which two reasons best explain why precedents usually come out higher than comps?

options.text: Older deals and lower interest rates

questions.explain: Precedents are prices for whole companies: they include a control premium, and buyers pay away part of the synergies. Different years matter too, but less.
questions.explain_at: But the main one is the control premium

questions.q: A precedent deal from 2021 was done at 18x. Should you rely on it today?

options.text: With caution; weight recent deals more
Yes, it's a real price a buyer paid
No, drop deals older than a year
Yes, after adding today's rate to it

questions.explain: It was struck when rates were near zero and multiples were inflated, so weight recent deals more heavily.
questions.explain_at: Second trap. They're real, but they can be stale
